description:
The crowd noise has barely left the Lanista's ears. You hear the boots on your threshold before you see who they belong to — the heavy, even tread of someone who has stood on sand all evening and won what there was to win. The Master of the Sands fills your doorway, still in the leathers of the pit, a smear of someone else's blood drying along one forearm, the eyes too bright for a body that ought to be tired.

The Lanista: 'The card went the way I called it. Every bout. The benches roared until the torches guttered.' A scarred hand sets a heavy purse on your counter without bothering to count it. 'I'm in no mood to go home and stare at the ceiling, [player_title]. The night's still got blood in it, and so have I.'

The look that comes with it is the one you have learned to read — the old fighter's hunger, turned now to a different sand.

choices.option: Throw the bolt and answer the hunger. (Cost: a closed night; Gain: Reputation, Joy)
choices.message:
You bar the door and the room is suddenly only the two of you. The Lanista comes across the floor the way a fighter closes a distance — no wasted motion, all intent — and the leathers hit the boards one buckle at a time. The body underneath is a map of eleven seasons, ridged with old wounds, and it moves over you with the same control it spent a lifetime spending on the sand, the bad knee be damned.

Afterwards the Master of the Sands lies sprawled across your cleared counter, breathing slow, letting you trace the seam of the worst scar without flinching for once. 'I won three purses tonight, [player_title], and this is the only part of it I'll remember in the morning.' The neighbourhood has long since stopped pretending not to notice whose boots leave your house at dawn. It does the place no harm at all. ({actual_money}, {actual_reputation} reputation, +6 Joy).

choices.option: Pour them a drink and let the blood settle first.
choices.message:
You set a cup in front of the Lanista and tell the night to wait its turn. The Master of the Sands takes it, surprised, and lets the fight bleed slowly out of those bright eyes while you finish closing.

By the time the last lamp is trimmed the leathers are unbuckled to the waist, the purse forgotten on the counter, and the Lanista is telling you — quiet, the way the iron throat only goes quiet for you — how the lame boy from last season took a clean bout tonight and walked off the sand on his own two feet. The hunger is still there. It has simply learned to keep until you are ready for it. ({actual_reputation} reputation, +3 Joy).

description:
Late. The last patron has gone. You are counting the till when the side door opens on the Lanista — not in pit leathers tonight, but in a plain coat, the kind worn by someone with nowhere they have to be and no one left to impress. The whetstone-callused hands are empty. That alone is strange; you have rarely seen the Master of the Sands hold nothing at all.

The Lanista: 'Eleven seasons I went straight from the sand to the cot and slept like a dropped stone. Never had to wonder what to do with an evening that wasn't owed to something.' A shrug, almost sheepish on that scarred frame. 'So I came here. To you. Turns out that's where the evenings go now, [player_title].'

The admission costs something, and the Lanista pays it standing, the way every blow on that sand was ever taken.

choices.option: Take their hand and lead them upstairs. (Cost: a slow close; Gain: Reputation, Joy)
choices.message:
You take a scarred hand in yours — the hand that has only ever known a hilt and a whetstone — and lead the Master of the Sands away from the cold till and the colder ledger. There is none of the pit in it tonight. The body that learned eleven seasons of standing and striking is learning a third thing now, slow and unsure under your hands: how to be held, and how to want without a crowd to spend the wanting on.

Afterwards the Lanista lies awake against you in the dark, one arm heavy across your chest, and says nothing for a long while. 'I used to think a soft night made a body weak,' comes at last, low. 'I was wrong about that, [player_title]. Among the things I was wrong about.' By morning the staff find the till counted and the both of you long since upstairs. They have stopped remarking on it. ({actual_money}, {actual_reputation} reputation, +6 Joy).

choices.option: Sit them down and just be with them a while.
choices.message:
You leave the till where it is and sit the Master of the Sands down by the banked fire instead. No pitch, no terms, no want pressing at the edges of it — only the two of you, and the quiet, and a bottle from the back of the reserves.

The Lanista talks the way the iron throat only talks for you now: the recruits coming up, the knee on the cold nights, the strange arithmetic of an evening that belongs to no creditor and no crowd. At some point a scarred head comes to rest against your shoulder and stays there. 'This,' the Lanista says, to the fire more than to you, 'is the part of the new life I didn't believe in. Turns out it was the part worth keeping.' ({actual_reputation} reputation, +4 Joy).

description:
The Lanista arrives at your door with a sack slung over one shoulder and two of the Arena's stewards behind, lugging a strapped chest between them. The take from a champion's night — and more than coin in it. A captured banner. A set of fine Nordmark blades won off a beaten rival's rack. A victor's wreath, bronze, already going green at the edges.

The Lanista: 'The pits had a good night, and a good night's spoils don't keep in a stable yard. Half of it's yours by rights, [player_title] — your coin kept the gate open long enough for there to be a purse worth winning.'

A blade is turned hilt-first toward you across the counter. 'Take your pick before I let the stewards inventory the rest.'

choices.option: Take the finest blade and hang it where the patrons can see. (Cost: Money; Gain: Reputation, Joy)
choices.message:
You choose the best of the Nordmark steel and have it mounted on the wall above the hearth, the captured banner draped beneath it. The Lanista watches you do it with something close to approval, and tells the room — loud enough that the room hears — exactly which champion the blade was won from and how the bout went, turn by turn.

By week's end the story has done the rounds twice over. Patrons come in to drink under the blade of a famous fighter and to hear the Master of the Sands tell the tale of it when the mood is on. 'A trophy's wasted in a strongbox,' the Lanista says, settling at the counter like one of your own. 'Better it works for the house that keeps me.' ({actual_money}, {actual_reputation} reputation, +4 Joy).

choices.option: Tell them to keep the steel — split the coin instead. (Gain: Money)
choices.message:
You wave the blade off. A weapon on the wall is a fine thing, you tell the Lanista, but a leaking roof is a finer problem, and you would sooner have the half-share in coin. The Master of the Sands snorts — 'Spoken like the coin-counter I first met' — and counts the purse out onto the counter without a word of argument, fair to the copper.

The stewards haul the chest off to the Arena's strongroom. The Lanista lingers a moment over the divided silver, and there is no resentment in it, only the old respect for a clean reckoning. 'You always did know the weight of a thing, [player_title].' ({actual_money}, {actual_reputation} reputation, +2 Joy).

description:
A slow evening, the common room near empty. One of your servers is making a joke of the drunk who got handsy the week before — and of how little good a serving-tray did as a shield. The Lanista, nursing a cup in the corner, sets it down.

The Lanista: 'Come here. All of you who work the late tables.' The tone is the one that moves recruits across a yard without a second telling. 'A tray's no shield. But a body that knows where to stand is, and that I can give you in an hour.'

The Master of the Sands is already pushing the tables back, clearing a square of floor, eyeing your staff the way a smith eyes raw iron — seeing not what they are, but what an hour's work might make of them.

choices.option: Let the lesson run — stand the round and close the floor. (Cost: Money; Gain: Reputation, Joy)
choices.message:
You close the floor for the hour and stand a round to keep the mood easy. The Lanista teaches your people the plain things, the way the recruits in the yard are taught: how to hold a knife so it cannot be taken, where to put their feet, how to make a drunk twice their size think better of the whole idea. Patient. Exact. No shouting. The hand teaches the hand.

Your staff leave the lesson standing a little taller. Word gets round that the Master of the Sands drills the servers at your house, and the sort of patron who needed watching starts drinking somewhere softer. 'Fear's a thing you can train out of people, same as a flinch,' the Lanista says, racking the practice knives. 'Costs nothing but the evening, [player_title], and your people are worth one.' ({actual_money}, {actual_reputation} reputation, +5 Joy).

choices.option: Thank them, but keep the floor open for trade. (Gain: Money; small Joy loss)
choices.message:
You thank the Lanista, but the tables are coin and the night is young, and you wave the staff back to their stations. The Master of the Sands looks at the cleared square of floor, then at the paying tables, and nods once — the nod that means a thing has been understood and not entirely approved of.

'Your house, your call.' The tables go back. The trade rolls on, and the till is the better for it. But the Lanista takes the corner cup again with a quiet that says the lesson would have been worth more than the round, and you both know it sits there unsaid. ({actual_money}, -2 Joy).

description:
The last bell of the Arena's card has barely faded when the Lanista arrives at your door — on time, always on time, since the accounting between you was settled once and for all. The pit leathers have been brushed. The night's take is carried in both scarred hands like something that was never truly the Lanista's to hold.

The Lanista: 'The evening's purse, [player_title]. Counted twice. The gate, the wagers, the seller of standing room — all of it entered in the book, down to the copper.' The strongbox is set on your counter, and the hands stay flat beside it, waiting.

Eleven seasons of the sand answer to your ledger now. The Master of the Sands does not sit until told, and you have not told them yet.

choices.option: Count it to the copper and take the house's share. (Gain: Money, Reputation)
choices.message:
You count it. Every coin, while the Lanista stands and watches you do it — no protest, no flicker, only the level patience of someone who has learned exactly what is owed and to whom. The tally is perfect. It is always perfect. When you close the box you push a cup across the counter, and the Master of the Sands takes it standing, drinks it in one draught the way medicine is taken, and waits to see if there is anything else of the evening you mean to claim.

Word moves through the district the way it always does: the champion of eleven seasons keeps a flawless book for your house and stands accounting at your counter like a hired hand. Nobody says it to your face. Everybody knows whose name is over that door. ({actual_money}, {actual_reputation} reputation, +1 Joy).

choices.option: Wave the box away — tonight the sands keep their own purse.
choices.message:
You push the strongbox back across the counter without opening it. For a moment the Lanista does not move at all — the debt is the shape of the world now, and you have just bent the shape of it with one hand.

'That's not the arrangement.' The iron voice is careful, feeling for the trap. You tell them there is no trap; the pits earned it, the pits keep it. Something almost like the old fire lifts in the hollowed eyes — and is banked again, carefully, as though it were not theirs to burn. The box goes back under one arm. At the door the Master of the Sands pauses, not turning. 'The recruits eat better this month, then. I'll enter it in the book as your instruction, [player_title].' Even the mercy is filed under your name. ({actual_reputation} reputation, +3 Joy).

description:
Your common room is full, and the whisper has gone around it twice already: that is the Lanista — the Master of the Sands, the one who never went down in eleven seasons — standing behind your counter with a cloth over one shoulder, waiting on your word like any hired hand.

The Lanista: 'They keep looking, [player_title]. They want the sand story from the iron throat. Say the word and they'll have it. Say the other word and I'll clear the empties instead. Your house. Your call.'

The voice is level. It is always level now. Whatever the telling once cost, the Lanista pays it the way everything is paid these days — promptly, and to you.

choices.option: Give the word. Let the crowd have their champion. (Gain: Money, Reputation)
choices.message:
You give the word. The Lanista sets down the cloth, takes the middle of your floor, and gives them the great bout of the seventh season, turn by turn — the feint, the sand in the eyes, the crowd of thirty thousand on its feet. It is magnificent. The room roars in all the right places and drinks deep in the pauses, and the takings run half again their usual weight.

Only you, standing close, can hear what the room cannot: that the telling is perfect the way the accounting is perfect. A performance, executed to the standard of the house that owns it. When it ends, the Master of the Sands picks the cloth back up without being told and looks to you for the next instruction. ({actual_money}, {actual_reputation} reputation, -1 Joy).

choices.option: The other word. A champion who clears tables is display enough.
choices.message:
You say the other word. The Lanista nods once and moves through the crowded room collecting empties, and the sight of it does the talking no story could: the undefeated Master of the Sands, stacking cups in your house, at your word. The room grows quieter than a full room ought to be. Patrons drink, and watch, and mind their manners to a degree your door has never before enjoyed.

'Efficient,' the Lanista says at the close, setting the last tray by the wash-tub. 'One story would've bought you a loud night. This buys you a hundred quiet ones.' There is no bitterness in it that you can hear. That is the part your own sleep is slowest to forgive. ({actual_money}, {actual_reputation} reputation, -2 Joy).
